::: {#sol-manual-backward}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
first, second = mlp[0], mlp[2]

# Forward, keeping every intermediate result.
z1 = x_train @ first.weight.T + first.bias
h = torch.relu(z1)
z2 = h @ second.weight.T + second.bias
loss = loss_fn(z2, y_train)

mlp.zero_grad()
loss.backward()

with torch.no_grad():
    # Backward, from the loss to the first layer, one row per image.
    g2 = (torch.softmax(z2, dim=1) - nn.functional.one_hot(y_train, 10)) / n_train
    grad_W2 = g2.T @ h
    grad_b2 = g2.sum(dim=0)
    grad_h = g2 @ second.weight
    grad_z1 = grad_h * (z1 > 0)
    grad_W1 = grad_z1.T @ x_train
    grad_b1 = grad_z1.sum(dim=0)

pairs = [(grad_W1, first.weight), (grad_b1, first.bias),
         (grad_W2, second.weight), (grad_b2, second.bias)]
backward_gap = max((mine - p.grad).abs().max().item() for mine, p in pairs)
print(backward_gap)
```

The four gradients match autograd's to within `r format(py$backward_gap, digits = 2)`.
The code runs the steps of @sol-loss-operations forward, then their derivatives in reverse:

- `g2` is $\gradwrt{\vz_2} L$ from @thm-ce-logit-grad, for every image at once,
  divided by `r py$n_train` because the loss is the mean over that many images;
- `grad_W2` and `grad_b2` are @sol-linear-param-grad, with the outer products of the images added up by one matrix product;
- `grad_h` is @sol-linear-input-grad, written for rows instead of columns;
- `grad_z1` is @sol-relu-grad;
- `grad_W1` and `grad_b1` are @sol-linear-param-grad again, for the first layer.

The backward steps reuse `z1` and `h` from the forward pass.

:::
